paras: The lynching of Robert Frye was the hanging of a man described as a horse thief, whose body was found in the woods near Arlington, Texas, on a Tuesday evening in mid-June 1881. His killers left a placard reading "Horse thief" on the body and were not identified. The killing reached distant readers only as a one-sentence item in national news-brief columns.

According to the Omaha Daily Bee, the dead body of "Bob Fryo", called "a no torious horsothiof" [a notorious horsethief], was found hanging in the woods near Arlington on Tuesday evening, which by the paper's 16 June date was 14 June. The body was "placarded 'Horsethief.'" The Delaware State Journal gave the name as Robert Frye and the place as "a forest near Arlington," adding that a card inscribed "Horse thief" was tied to his neck. Neither account says when or where Frye was seized, how many men took part, or what theft he was accused of.
"The lynchers are unknown," the Delaware State Journal reported. No report of an inquest, arrests or prosecution appears in the coverage.

The Omaha Daily Bee ran the item on 16 June among brief telegraphic notes on page one, and the Delaware State Journal of Wilmington printed a fuller version on 23 June in its "In General" column. Both papers stated Frye's alleged horse stealing as fact rather than as an accusation and offered no comment on the hanging. Neither mentioned his race; the same Delaware column also reported, in a separate item, the lynching of "a colored man named Ruse" at Weston, Missouri. No account from a Texas paper was found in the coverage.

bases: Both reports say Frye was found hanged in woods near Arlington with a 'Horse thief' placard, and A2 attributes the killing to unknown 'lynchers' [A1, A2].

Frye was found hanged with a placard naming him a horse thief, and A2 calls the killers 'lynchers', which marks an extralegal killing on a crime pretext [A1, A2]. Neither paper gives the number of killers, so a group of three or more is implied by the word 'lynchers' but not stated [A2].
Two short national news briefs carry the story [A1, A2]; they agree on the core facts but both appear to derive from one Texas dispatch, and no local or follow-up report was found.
